item.title: [CBS News World] Leaked data shows 490,000 Russian forces have died in Ukraine war
item.description:
More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died since Vladimir Putin ordered Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, according to leaked Russian government data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News. Another organization's analysis of the vast dataset suggests the toll is likely closer to 700,000.
A recent hack by pro-Ukraine groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow produced the data that was analyzed by the BBC and independent Russian outlet Mediazona. It included more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, according to the British broadcaster.
The data, which includes granular information on the location of deaths in Ukraine and Russian border regions, age ranges, causes of death, and employment and court rulings suggests at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died during the war so far, according to the BBC. According to Mediazona's analysis, which the outlet said accounted for delays in death registrations, missing records and deaths occurring since the data was leaked, Russia's total military death toll has likely reached around 700,000.
In May, the head of the United Kingdom's communications and cyber spy agency also put the number of Russian military deaths during the war at about 500,000, citing Western intelligence.
"Putin is going backwards on the battlefield, with new intelligence showing that almost half a million Russian soldiers have been killed since the conflict began," Anne Keast-Butler, the director of the Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), said at the time.

item.title: [ABC News World] Migration to Spain's Canary Islands breaks day record with nearly 2,000 arrivals
item.description:
Migration to Spain's Canary Islands breaks day record with nearly 2,000 arrivals
Spanish authorities report nearly 2,000 migrants arrived at the Canary Islands on Tuesday, setting a record for a single dayByJOSEPH WILSON Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 5:48 AM
BARCELONA, Spain -- Spanish authorities said nearly 2,000 migrants arrived at Spain’s Canary Islands on Tuesday, a record high for migrants reaching the archipelago on a single day.
The islands located off the coast of West Africa saw a surge in arrivals just before Spain holds a national election later this week, when migration will be a major concern for many voters.
Spain’s maritime rescue service said that 1,990 people arrived on 15 different boats as search and rescue vessels accompanied one dinghy after another to the small island of El Hierro.
“Sadly, this is a historic day,” the Canary Islands' regional leader Fernando Clavijo said in an interview with Spanish radio Cadena Ser.
There were around 100 minors among Tuesday’s arrivals, including a four-day-old baby that had been born during the journey, Clavijo said.
The Canary Islands, a tourist hotspot for many Europeans drawn to its year-round mild weather, have for years been a key entry point for migrants desperate to reach Europe. The route is also extremely dangerous with thousands dying in the attempted crossing.
Although the islands lie about 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the nearest African coast, many migrants take longer routes to evade security forces. The journeys can last days or weeks, with many boats missing their target and drifting into the open Atlantic.
Over 26,000 people have reached the Canary Islands this year, with half that total coming in November. The previous single-day record was hit just two weeks before, when 1,400 people arrived at Gran Canaria on Nov. 7.

item.title: [ABC News World] Cambodia hosts Chinese military for largest Golden Dragon joint exercise yet
item.description:
Cambodia hosts Chinese military for largest Golden Dragon joint exercise yet
Cambodia and China have started joint military exercises aimed at strengthening cooperation between Beijing and its closest political partner in Southeast AsiaBySOPHENG CHEANG Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 6:00 AM
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- China and Cambodia launched their eighth joint military exercise on Wednesday, seeking to strengthen ties between Beijing and its closest political partner in Southeast Asia. Cambodian military spokesperson Thong Solimo said the drills are the largest since the exercise began in 2016.
The 15-day Golden Dragon-2026 exercise will end on Dec. 9. Its stated focus is counterterrorism, humanitarian assistance, anti-piracy operations and disaster relief.
The drills are part of Beijing’s broader push to expand its regional influence. Cambodia consistently backs Chinese foreign policy, while Beijing is its most important ally and benefactor. Chinese aid and investment have helped fuel Cambodia’s rapid economic growth in recent decades.
The United States, China’s main rival for influence in the region, has expressed concern over the military ties between Beijing and Phnom Penh. Cambodia suspended its joint Angkor Sentinel exercise with the United States in 2017, after the last drills in 2016. Following efforts by both sides to improve military relations, the exercise is set to resume next February.
Beijing has helped fund an expansion of the Ream Naval Base on Cambodia’s southern coast, raising concerns it could become a strategic outpost for the Chinese navy in the Gulf of Thailand. Cambodia has repeatedly denied any agreement granting China special privileges or the establishment of a foreign military base.

item.description:
Pope Leo laments lack of climate commitments after UN talks end without agreement
Pope Leo XIV has expressed concern over the failure of United Nations climate talks to reach an agreementBySILVIA STELLACCI Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 5:53 AM
VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Wednesday expressed concern over the failure of United Nations climate talks to reach an agreement, saying that “extreme environmental events linked to the climate crisis are becoming increasingly frequent.”
The pope has embraced defense of the environment in his papacy, taking up one of the core teachings of his predecessor, Pope Francis, whose landmark encyclical Laudato Si (Praised Be) cast care for the planet as an urgent, existential moral concern.
Leo issued an appeal during his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square to “never forget the human face of the climate crisis, which affects the lives of millions of people, strikes entire communities and undermines the prospects of future generations.”
He called for “fundamental changes in behavior, socioeconomic systems and the governance of our societies,” directing his appeal to “the international community and to each individual.”

item.title: [NPR News] Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor
item.description:
Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor
November 25, 20266:00 AM ET
Emily Feng
Emily Feng/NPR
As dawn broke one recent morning over camp, we got one of our first full views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, normally hidden behind clouds.
Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts. The beating sun bakes you during the day, walking so close to the equator, but the nights quickly dip below freezing. Snow remains constantly in sight from humid rainforest and alpine landscapes, freshly charred from a wildfire three weeks before. And always beckoning is the peak, within sight, but seemingly never nearer; the high altitude means hikers need to walk slowly or else risk exhaustion and altitude sickness.
A group of friends and fellow hikers and I spent days camping at altitude to acclimatize before a final summit push during our second-to-last evening on the mountain. We trudged through heavy snow under the stars, cresting a massive volcanic crater rim, and leaned against drifts of what had become a full blizzard to reach the top in the early morning hours. I stood on the peak I'd seen only from a distance for the last week but saw only whiteness: all snow and ice, the absence of life and color heightened by my low oxygen levels.

item.description:
Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long hostage siege, with the president saying all of those held hostage had been rescued and one captor killed.
Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to have been held by armed men.
"In an extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the Armed Forces, all the hostages were rescued," President Abelardo de la Espriella said in a video posted on social media.
A Colombian Army soldier is seen in the Exito Supermarket after security forces stormed the building to free hostages held by gunmen in Cartagena, Colombia, in the early hours of Nov. 25, 2026.
AFP via Getty Images
Shortly after midnight, a police helicopter hovered low over the shopping center as security forces massed outside the supermarket, AFP reporters saw.
Explosions then echoed around the complex as tactical teams moved in.
Ten of the roughly 30 people initially held had been released during the 17-hour standoff, including several elderly women.
Moments later, soldiers could be seen inside the Exito supermarket as security forces secured the building.
De la Espriella, who appeared at the scene wearing fatigues and a sidearm while brandishing a walkie-talkie, described the operation as a roaring success.
"We gave them the opportunity to surrender and free the hostages. They rejected that opportunity and we acted decisively," he said, lauding the operation as "absolutely flawless."

item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Chen Jining was a rising star in the Chinese Communist PartyByKoh EwePublished6 hours ago
Chinese authorities are investigating Shanghai's party chief, a rising star in the Communist Party, as part of Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption drive.
Chen Jining, 62, is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws", according to a statement published on Tuesday by the party's anti-corruption body.
Chen is now the fourth member of the elite Politburo to be investigated, in the widest purge yet of the party's top executive body since the end of the Cultural Revolution.
As the party prepares to appoint fresh leaders at next year's National People's Congress, uncertainty looms over what its new command will look like - except that Xi will remain at the helm.
Before Chen, three other members of the current Politburo - appointed in 2022 - were investigated and subsequently expelled: ex-generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.
While Chen has not been removed from the Politburo, it's rare for officials to return after such investigations.
"Who on this Politburo feels safe, especially as the personnel machinations for next year's Party Congress intensify?" China analyst Bill Bishop wrote in his Sinocism newsletter.
Chen's investigation came as a surprise, according to Bishop, given rumours were swirling that another senior official, not Chen, would fall next in the anti-corruption campaign.
The role of Shanghai party chief, which Chen assumed in 2022, is known to be a prestigious springboard to the country's top office.
Chen's long list of predecessors include former president Jiang Zemin, his premier Zhu Rongji, incumbent premier Li Qiang and Xi Jinping himself.

item.title: [BBC World] Russia's own figures show it has lost almost 500,000 people in Ukraine war
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiersByOlga Ivshina and Yaroslava Kiryukhina, BBC RussianPublished25 November 2026, 00:56 GMT
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.
Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.
The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.

Watch: BBC reporter investigates deaths of family members in Russia-Ukraine warByAnastasiya Gribanova BBC Eye Investigations Published25 November 2026, 00:54 GMT
I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.
The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.
Image caption,
The photo Anastasiya was sent of her grandparents' graves
I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.
"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said.
It turned my world upside down.
Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.
We stopped speaking.
Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.
Image source, Gribanova family handoutImage caption,
Anastasiya (bottom left) with her father (top left) and grandparents (right) before the war
Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.
After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.

item.description:

A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to NvidiaByLaura BickerChina correspondent Published24 November 2026
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Trunmp and Xi ahead of their meeting in Shenzhen last week
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.
